title: RAG Evaluation: Precision, Recall, Faithfulness, RAGAS Explained Clearly
description:
Evaluating RAG systems requires more than checking how similar an answer is to a reference.
Traditional metrics like BLEU, ROUGE, and F1 measure wording, coverage, and factual correctness, but RAG introduces a new layer through retrieval and grounding.

In this video, we break down the full evaluation pipeline for RAG systems.
We explore context precision, context recall, answer relevance, faithfulness, groundedness, and how LLM-as-a-Judge fits into modern evaluation.

Finally, we look at RAGAS, the open-source framework that standardizes these evaluations using embeddings and LLM-based scoring.

This video is designed for engineers, researchers, and anyone building retrieval-augmented generation systems who wants a clear and structured understanding of how to measure quality end-to-end.

So, let's get started. Let's start with
traditional evaluation matrix. Blue or
bilingual evaluation under study
measures how many engrams in the
generated text also appears in the
reference text. A 1 g is a single word.
A 2 g is a pair of words and so on. Blue
checks these overlaps and produces a
score between zero and one. A higher
score means the generated sentence
closely follows the reference. For
example, take the reference, the sky is
blue today. And the output, the sky
looks blue today. In the output, four
out of the five 1 gs, the sky, blue, and
today match the reference. So the 1 g
precision becomes 4th or 0.8
for the two gs. Two out of the four
pairs, the sky and blue today also match
the reference. So the 2 g precision
becomes almost half. Blue then takes the
geometric mean of these precision and
gives a combined score of about 0.63.
Both sentences have the same length. So
the brevity penalty equals. Now brevity
penalty is always between 0 and one. and
it simply reduces the blue score when
the generated sentence is shorter than
the reference. So the final blue score
for this example stays around 0.63.
This is why blue became the standard for
machine translation where these short
word patterns are a strong signal of
equality. All right. Next let's discuss
rouge or recall oriented understudy for
gisting evaluation. It measures how much
of the reference content appears in the
generated output. Instead of focusing on
matching phrases exactly, Rouge focuses
on recall. That is how much of the
important information is captured. This
makes rouge especially useful for
summarization where the phrasing can
change but the core ideas must stay
intact. For example, consider the
reference summary. The company achieved
record profits and the generated
summary. Record profits were reported
this quarter. To calculate rouge one, we
look at 1 g overlap. The keywords record
and profits appear in both. So the
generated summary captures two out of
the three important content words in the
reference. That gives us a rouge one
recall of 2x3 which is around 0.66.
For rouge two, we look at two gram
overlap. The reference has the pair
record profits. The generated summary
also contains the same pair. So, rouge
two recall becomes one out of one, which
is one. Since the generated summary
captures the main idea even with
different phrasing, rouge assigns a
strong score. This is why rouge became
the go-to metric for summarization where
meaning matters more than matching
sentences word for word.
All right. Now, let's look at F1 score.
It measures how many important elements
in the generated answer match the
reference. It works using precision and
recall and then combines them into a
single number. Precision tells us how
many of the predicted items are correct.
Recalls tells us how many of the correct
items were captured. F1 is the harmonic
mean of these two giving a balanced
score. This makes F1 useful for tasks
where the correctness of specific pieces
of information matters more than full
sentence structure like question
answering, extraction and
classification.
For example, take the question who
discovered penicellin. Reference answer
is Alexander Fleming and the generated
answer is Flleaming discovered it in
1928. Here the key element we care about
is the entity Fleming which refers to
the same person as Alexander Fleming.
The model predicted one entity Fleming
and it is correct. So the precision is
one and the reference expected one
entity Alexander Fleming which is also
present in the output. So the recall is
also one. Combining these F1 becomes
one. Even though the sentence is phrased
differently, the correct factual element
is present. So the F1 score is perfect.
This makes F1 a strong metric for
evaluating tasks where capturing the
right fact or entity is more important
than matching the entire sentences.
Okay. So traditional matrix like blue,
rouge and F1 work well when there is a
fixed reference answer and the goal is
to match its wording or important
elements.
They are perfect for translation,
summarization and extraction. But a rag
system works differently. It retrieves
information first and then generates an
answer from that information. So the
quality of the final answer depends on
both the retrieval step and the
generation step. Because of this
similarity based matrix are not enough.
A rag system needs matrix that directly
evaluate how relevant the retrieved
context is, how well the answer uses
that context and how accurately the
answer responds to the question. This
brings us to the matrix that are used
specifically for evaluating rag systems.
So the first matrix here is context
precision. Context precision measures
how much of the retrieved context is
actually relevant to the question. If
the system retrieves five chunks and
only two out of them are useful, the
precision is two out of five. A higher
precision means the retriever brought in
less noise. Example, if the query is who
founded Tesla and the retriever brings
five chunks but only two talk about Elon
Musk and Tesla's founding, then the
context precision is 2 out of five which
is 0.4. It tells us that the retriever
pulled some relevant information but
also a lot of unrelated content.
Next, let's discuss context recall. It
measures how much of the relevant
information the retriever managed to
find. If there are three important
chunks in the database and the retriever
finds two of them, the recall is two out
of three. Example, for the same query,
if there are three chunks that contain
the founding details of Tesla and the
retriever returns two out of them, the
recall is 2x3 which is 0.66.
It shows the retriever captured most of
the required information but missed one
useful chunk.
All right. Now let's discuss answer
relevance. Answer relevance measures how
directly the generated answer responds
to the user's question. This is usually
done using embeddings to check how
closely the answer aligns with the
query's meaning. For example, the
question, what is a transformer model?
We get a answer. A transformer is a
neural network architecture based on
attention. Both are semantically close.
So, relevance will be high. Next one is
faithfulness. Faithfulness checks
whether the answer is fully supported by
the retrieved context. If a statement in
the answer does not appear in the
retrieved text, faithfulness goes down.
For example, if the retrieved context
mentions Tesla's founders and the answer
adds a claim that isn't present in those
chunks, faithfulness drops because the
answer is no longer grounded in the
provided evidence.
And the last one which we are going to
discuss here is groundedness.
Groundedness measures how well the
answer uses the retrieved context
instead of relying on the model's
internal memory. If the answer copies or
closely paraphrases relevant parts of
retrieved documents, groundedness is
high. For example, if the retrieved
chunk says Fleming discovered
penicelline in 1928 and the answer says
penicelline was discovered by Fleming in
The grounding score is high because the
answer is clearly based on the given
evidence.
These rag evaluation matrix like context
precision, context recall, answer
relevance, faithfulness and groundedness
give a good understanding of how well
the system retrieved information and how
accurately it used that information. But
in practice, calculating these scores
consistently is not always simple. Some
of them can be computed with embeddings,
but others need deeper reasoning. For
example, to check faithfulness, an
evaluator has to read the question. the
retrieved context and the answer
together and decide whether the answer
is fully supported. This is where LLM as
a judge becomes useful. A large language
model can act like an evaluator. It
reads everything, the query, the
retrieved chunks and the final answer
and then gives a score for grounding or
relevance. Very similar to how a human
would judge equality. To make all of
this easier and standardize, the
community built Ragas, a dedicated
open-source framework for evaluating rag
systems.
Ragas provide a structured way to
compute rag evaluation matrix without
manually building evaluators for each
one. It uses embeddings for semantic
comparisons and it uses LLM as a judge
for evaluations that require deeper
understanding.
This helps capture meaning, grounding
and factual alignment even when the
wording varies. Raas provides four main
scores. Faithfulness which is whether
the answer is fully supported by the
retrieved context. Answer relevance
which checks how well the answer
addresses the question. context
precision which checks how much of the
retrieved context is actually relevant
and context recall which tells how much
of the relevant information was
successfully retrieved. These four
matrix together give a clear and
consistent picture of rag system
quality.
Rag system needs evaluation methods that
look beyond surface level text
similarity. Traditional matrix like
blue, rouge and f1 helps us understand
wording, coverage and factual elements.
But rag adds another layer through
retrieval and grounding. Matrix such as
context precision, context recall,
answer relevance and faithfulness help
evaluate these two steps clearly and
frameworks like Ragas bring these
evaluation together into a simple
consistent workflow supported by
techniques like embeddings and LLM as a
judge. With these tools, it becomes
straightforward to identify where a rag
system is strong and where it needs
improvement. So that's all on rag
evaluation. Thanks for watching. This is
Logical Lenses. See you in the next one.
